hello.title: Hello, JavaScript
hello.summary: Write your first program, print text and numbers with console.log and learn what a statement is.
hello.lesson.0: JavaScript is the language of the web. Every browser can run it, and with Node.js it also runs on your computer and on servers. A program is a list of instructions that the computer runs from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.1: To show something on the screen, you use `console.log()`. Put the value you want to show between the parentheses.
hello.lesson.4: Each instruction is a **statement**. You end a statement with a semicolon `;` and usually write one statement per line. The program runs the lines in order.
hello.lesson.7: Text in quotes is a **string**. You can use double quotes `"Hi"` or single quotes `'Hi'`. Numbers have no quotes. JavaScript can calculate with them: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies and `/` divides.
hello.lesson.9: `console.log()` can show several values at once. Separate them with commas. It prints them on one line with a space between them. Note the difference: `"2 + 3"` is a string, so it is printed as it is.
hello.lesson.11: A **comment** starts with `//`. JavaScript ignores everything after `//` until the end of the line. In this course, comments only show results, for example `// 5`.
hello.lesson.12: JavaScript is **case-sensitive**. `console.log` works, but `Console.log` or `console.Log` stops the program with an error.
hello.card.0: `console.log(x)` prints a value on its own line
hello.card.1: `"Hi"` and `'Hi'` are strings, `42` is a number
hello.card.3: End statements with `;`, comments start with `//`
hello-1.explain: `console.log()` prints a value. The other lines cause an error in JavaScript.
hello-2.explain: There are no quotes, so `4 + 5` is a calculation and the result `9` is printed.
hello-3.explain: The value is in quotes, so it is a string. A string is printed exactly as it is written.
hello-4.explain: A program runs from top to bottom, so it prints `A` first and then `B`.
hello-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `Hi`.
hello-5.explain: The method that prints a value is `console.log()`.
hello-6.prompt: Build a line that prints `Score: 10` with two values.
hello-6.explain: Values separated by a comma are printed with a space between them: `console.log("Score:", 10);`.
hello-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Ready`, then `Set`, then `Go!`.
hello-7.explain: The lines run from top to bottom, so the first line to print must come first.
hello-8.prompt: Match the code to what it is.
hello-9.explain: The string `"Middle` has no closing quote. The fix is `console.log("Middle");`.
hello-10.explain: `2 * 6` has no quotes, so it is calculated. `console.log` puts a space between the two values.
hello-11.explain: `30 + 1` is calculated first. Then both values are printed with a space between them.
hello-12.explain: JavaScript is case-sensitive. `Console` with a capital C does not exist, so the program stops with an error.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values with let and const and meet the basic types: number, string, boolean, undefined and null.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value. You create one with `let`, a name, `=` and a value. After that, you use the name instead of the value. Names with several words are usually written in **camelCase**, like `firstName`.
variables.lesson.2: A variable created with `let` can change. To give it a new value, write the name, `=` and the new value, without `let`. The old value is gone. The new value can use the old one.
variables.lesson.5: Use `const` for a value that never changes. If you assign a new value to a `const`, the program stops with a `TypeError`. Many programmers use `const` by default and `let` only when the value must change.
variables.lesson.8: Every value has a **type**. A `number` is any number, with or without a decimal point. A `string` is text. A `boolean` is either `true` or `false`.
variables.lesson.9: Two special values mean that there is no value. `undefined` is the value of a variable that did not get a value yet. `null` is a value you set on purpose to say: empty.
variables.lesson.11: The `typeof` operator gives you the type of a value, as a string.
variables.lesson.13: `typeof null` gives `"object"`. This is an old mistake in JavaScript that can no longer be changed. Remember that `null` is a type of its own.
variables.card.0: `let x = 5;` creates a variable you can change
variables.card.1: `const y = 10;` creates a variable that cannot change
variables.card.3: `typeof x` gives the type as a string, e.g. `"number"`
variables-1.explain: `a` starts as `3`. Then `a = a + 4` stores `3 + 4`, which is `7`.
variables-2.prompt: Which keyword creates a variable that cannot get a new value?
variables-2.explain: A `const` cannot get a new value. A `let` variable can change, and `fixed` is not a JavaScript keyword.
variables-3.explain: The value is in quotes, so `"42"` is a string, not a number.
variables-4.explain: The variable has no value yet, so it is `undefined`, not `0`.
variables-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `boolean`.
variables-5.explain: `true` without quotes is a boolean. `"true"` is a string, `null` gives `"object"` and `1` is a number.
variables-6.explain: Names are case-sensitive. There is no variable `Total`, only `total`. The fix is `console.log(total);`.
variables-7.prompt: Match each value to its meaning.
variables-8.explain: `let y = x` copies the value `5` into `y`. Changing `x` later does not change `y`.
variables-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `12`.
variables-9.explain: A variable must be created before you use it. `points` needs `base`, and the print comes after the change.
variables-10.prompt: Build a line that creates a constant named `city` with the value `"Rome"`.
variables-10.explain: A constant is created with `const`, the name, `=` and the value: `const city = "Rome";`. Text needs quotes.
variables-11.explain: `message` has no value yet, so its value and its type are both `undefined`.
variables-12.explain: `typeof null` gives `"object"`. This is an old mistake in JavaScript.
operators.title: Operators and strings
operators.summary: Calculate with numbers, compare values with === and !==, and build and change strings.
operators.lesson.0: JavaScript has the usual **arithmetic operators**: `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. The operator `%` gives the remainder of a division, and `**` raises a number to a power: `2 ** 3` is `8`. `*` and `/` are calculated before `+` and `-`, like in math.
operators.lesson.2: `x += 5` is a short form of `x = x + 5`. It also works with `-=`, `*=` and `/=`. `x++` adds `1` to `x`, and `x--` subtracts `1`.
operators.lesson.5: `===` checks if two values are equal and gives `true` or `false`. `!==` checks if they are different. `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare sizes.
operators.lesson.7: Always use `===` and `!==`. The older `==` changes the types before it compares, so `5 == "5"` is `true`. This causes bugs that are hard to find.
operators.lesson.9: `+` joins strings. A **template literal** is often easier: write the string between backticks and put values inside `${...}`. JavaScript puts the value in place.
operators.lesson.11: `length` is the number of characters in a string. `word[0]` is the first character, because positions start at `0`. Strings also have **methods**, which you call with a dot, like `toUpperCase()`. They return a new string and do not change the original.
operators.lesson.13: `+` with a string and a number joins them as text. `"5" + 2` gives `"52"`, not `7`.
operators-1.explain: `17` divided by `5` is `3` with a remainder of `2`. `%` gives the remainder.
operators-2.explain: In a template literal, `${city}` is replaced by the value of `city`.
operators-3.explain: `"5"` is a string. `+` with a string joins the values as text, so the result is `"52"`.
operators-4.explain: `===` also compares the types. `10` is a number and `"10"` is a string, so the result is `false`.
operators-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `true`.
operators-5.explain: `4` and `9` are different, so `a !== b` is `true`. The other two give `false`.
operators-6.prompt: Build a line that stores the length of `name` in `size`.
operators-6.explain: `length` is a property of the string, so you write `name.length`: `const size = name.length;`.
operators-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Total: 12`.
operators-7.explain: First create `total`, then add `2`. Only then build the text and print it.
operators-8.prompt: Match the operator to its meaning.
operators-9.prompt: The program should print `Hello, Sam!`. Which line has the bug?
operators-9.explain: `${name}` only works in a template literal. Write the string between backticks instead of double quotes.
operators-11.explain: `*` is calculated before `+`: `3 * 4` is `12`, and `2 + 12` is `14`.
operators-12.explain: Positions start at `0`. `word[0]` is `"c"`, so `word[1]` is `"a"`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program choose with if and else, combine conditions with && and ||, and learn what truthy and falsy mean.
conditions.lesson.0: An `if` statement runs code only when a condition is `true`. Write the condition in parentheses and the code in curly braces `{ }`.
conditions.lesson.2: Add `else` for code that runs when the condition is `false`. With `else if`, you can check more conditions one after the other. Only the first block whose condition is `true` runs.
conditions.lesson.5: **Logical operators** combine conditions. `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are `true`. `||` (or) is `true` when at least one side is `true`. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.
conditions.lesson.8: The **ternary operator** `condition ? a : b` is a short `if` and `else` that gives a value. The value is `a` if the condition is `true`, otherwise `b`.
conditions.lesson.11: A condition does not have to be a boolean. These values count as `false` and are called **falsy**: `false`, `0`, `""` (an empty string), `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` (not a number). All other values are **truthy**, even `"0"` and `"false"`. `Boolean(x)` shows you which one a value is.
conditions.lesson.13: Indent the code inside `{ }` by two spaces. JavaScript does not need it, but it makes your code much easier to read.
conditions-1.explain: `7 % 2` is `1`, not `0`, so the condition is `false` and the `else` block runs.
conditions-2.explain: `15 > 20` is `false`, `15 > 10` is `true`. Only the first block whose condition is `true` runs.
conditions-3.explain: `&&` is only `true` when both sides are `true`.
conditions-4.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `Welcome`.
conditions-4.explain: `||` is `true` when at least one side is `true`. `isGuest` is `true`, so the condition is `true`.
conditions-5.explain: `0` is falsy, so the ternary operator gives the second value.
conditions-6.prompt: The program should print `Weekend`. Which line has the bug?
conditions-6.explain: A day cannot be Saturday and Sunday at the same time, so `&&` is always `false`. Use `||` instead.
conditions-7.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
conditions-7.pairs.3: a short if and else that gives a value
conditions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Win` when `points` is greater than `50`, otherwise `Lose`.
conditions-8.explain: The `if` line opens the first block, `} else {` closes it and opens the second one, and `}` closes the second one.
conditions-9.prompt: Build a line that stores `"yes"` in `answer` when `ok` is truthy, otherwise `"no"`.
conditions-9.explain: The ternary operator is `condition ? a : b`: `const answer = ok ? "yes" : "no";`.
conditions-10.prompt: Which of these values is truthy?
conditions-10.explain: `"0"` is a string that is not empty, so it is truthy. `0`, `""` and `null` are falsy.
conditions-11.explain: `5 > 3` is `true`, but `10 < 10` is `false`. With `&&`, both sides must be `true`.
conditions-12.explain: `"false"` is a string that is not empty, so it is truthy.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with for, while and for...of, and control loops with break and continue.
loops.lesson.0: A **loop** repeats code. The `for` loop is the most common one. Its parentheses have three parts, separated by semicolons: a start (`let i = 1`), a condition (`i <= 3`) and a step (`i++`).
loops.lesson.2: First, the loop runs the start. Then it checks the condition, runs the code in the braces and runs the step. It repeats this until the condition is `false`. A common pattern adds up values in a variable that you create before the loop.
loops.lesson.5: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. Use it when you do not know in advance how many times the loop must run.
loops.lesson.7: Make sure that the condition becomes `false` at some point. If it never does, the loop runs forever and your program does not stop.
loops.lesson.9: `for...of` goes through the items of a collection, one by one. With a string, you get each character. You will use it a lot in the world about arrays.
loops.lesson.12: `break` stops the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next round.
loops.card.2: `for (const x of items) { ... }` goes through each item
loops.card.3: `break` stops the loop, `continue` skips to the next round
loops-1.prompt: How many times does this print `Hi`?
loops-1.explain: `i` takes the values `2`, `3`, `4`, `5` and `6`. That is 5 rounds.
loops-2.explain: The loop adds `1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5` to `total`, which is `15`.
loops-3.explain: `n` becomes `3`, then `9`, then `27`. Now `27 < 20` is `false`, so the loop stops.
loops-4.explain: When `i` is `2`, `break` stops the whole loop. The program only prints `0` and `1`.
loops-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the loop prints `5`, `4`, `3`, `2` and `1`.
loops-5.explain: `i--` subtracts `1` in every round. `i -= 2` skips numbers, and `i++` never makes the condition `false`.
loops-6.prompt: The program should print `1`, `2` and `3`. Which line has the bug?
loops-6.explain: `i--` makes `i` smaller, so `i <= 3` stays `true` forever. The fix is `i++;`.
loops-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `6`.
loops-7.explain: Create `sum` before the loop, add inside the loop, and print after the loop. Otherwise it prints more than once.
loops-8.prompt: Match the code to what it does.
loops-9.prompt: Build the first line of a loop that counts from `0` to `4`.
loops-9.explain: `i < 5` is `true` for `0` to `4`. With `i <= 5`, the loop would also count `5`.
loops-10.explain: `for...of` gives one character per round, and every `console.log` prints on its own line.
loops-11.explain: `continue` skips every number that cannot be divided by `3`. Only `3`, `6` and `9` are counted.
loops-12.statement: A `while` loop whose condition is `false` at the start never runs its code.
loops-12.explain: `while` checks the condition before every round, also before the first one.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write reusable code with functions: parameters, return values, arrow functions and default parameters.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a named block of code that you can run again and again. You define it with `function`, a name, parentheses and the code in curly braces. You run it by **calling** it: its name followed by `()`.
functions.lesson.2: **Parameters** are names in the parentheses of the function. They get the values that you pass when you call the function. These values are called **arguments**.
functions.lesson.5: `return` sends a value back to the place where the function was called. The function stops at `return`. A function without `return` gives `undefined`.
functions.lesson.7: `console.log` only shows a value. It does not give the value back. If you want to use the result of a function, use `return`.
functions.lesson.9: An **arrow function** is a shorter way to write a function. You usually store it in a `const`. If the code is a single expression, you can leave out the curly braces and `return`. The value is then returned automatically.
functions.lesson.12: A **default parameter** has a value that is used when the call leaves out the argument. Write it with `=` after the parameter name.
functions.card.2: `const f = (x) => x * 2;` is an arrow function
functions-2.explain: The arguments go to the parameters in order: `a` is `3` and `b` is `8`, so `a - b` is `-5`.
functions-3.explain: `show(5)` prints `5`, but it has no `return`. So `value` is `undefined`, and that is printed next.
functions-4.explain: The function stops at `return`, so the line after it never runs.
functions-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `8`.
functions-5.explain: `return` gives the result back to the call. With `console.log`, the function would return `undefined`.
functions-6.prompt: Build an arrow function `half` that divides a number by 2.
functions-6.explain: An arrow function with one expression needs no braces and no `return`: `const half = (n) => n / 2;`.
functions-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Hi, Sam`.
functions-7.explain: The arrow function must be created before you call it. Its code goes between `{` and `};`.
functions-8.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
functions-9.prompt: The program should print `20`. Which line has the bug?
functions-9.explain: The function calculates the value but does not give it back, so it returns `undefined`. The fix is `return width * height;`.
functions-10.explain: When you leave out `count`, its default value `1` is used.
functions-11.explain: The call has no argument, so `name` gets its default value `"friend"`.
functions-12.statement: `const f = (x) => x + 1;` returns `x + 1` without the word `return`.
functions-12.explain: An arrow function without curly braces returns the value of its expression automatically.
arrays.title: Arrays
arrays.summary: Keep many values in one list: read and change items, add and remove them, and transform arrays with map and filter.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** is an ordered list of values. You write it with square brackets `[ ]` and separate the items with commas. `console.log` shows the whole array, and `length` is the number of items.
arrays.lesson.2: Each item has an **index**, its position. The first item has index `0`, the second has index `1`, and so on. The last item has index `length - 1`. You can also change an item through its index.
arrays.lesson.4: You can change the items of an array in a `const`. `const` only means that the variable always holds the same array.
arrays.lesson.6: `push()` adds an item at the end. `pop()` removes the last item and returns it. `includes()` checks if an item is in the array.
arrays.lesson.9: `for...of` gives you each item. The method `forEach()` does the same with a function: it calls the function once for every item.
arrays.lesson.11: `map()` creates a **new** array: it calls a function for every item and keeps the results. `filter()` creates a new array with only the items for which the function returns `true`. The original array does not change.
arrays.card.0: `const a = [1, 2, 3];` and `a[0]` is the first item
arrays.card.4: `a.forEach((x) => console.log(x))` runs code for each item
arrays-1.explain: Indexes start at `0`: `"a"` is `0`, `"b"` is `1` and `"c"` is `2`.
arrays-2.explain: The array starts with 3 items. `push()` adds one more, so `length` is `4`.
arrays-3.explain: `filter()` keeps the items for which `n > 4` is `true`, in their original order.
arrays-4.explain: The array has the indexes `0` and `1`. There is no item at index `2`, so it prints `undefined`.
arrays-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `[ 1, 4, 9 ]`.
arrays-5.explain: `map()` makes a new array with the result for every item. `forEach()` returns `undefined`, and `filter()` only keeps or drops items.
arrays-6.prompt: Build a line that creates `long`, an array with the words of `words` that have more than 3 letters.
arrays-6.explain: `filter()` keeps the items for which the function returns `true`: `const long = words.filter((w) => w.length > 3);`.
arrays-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `[ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]`.
arrays-7.explain: `push()` adds at the end, so `"b"` must be added before `"c"`.
arrays-8.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
arrays-8.pairs.4: checks if `x` is in the array
arrays-9.prompt: The program should print the last fruit, `plum`. Which line has the bug?
arrays-9.explain: The last index is `length - 1`, because indexes start at `0`. The fix is `fruits[fruits.length - 1]`.
arrays-10.explain: `map()` returns a new array and does not change the original. `b` is `[ 2, 3, 4 ]`, but `a` stays the same.
arrays-11.explain: `pop()` removes the last item and returns it.
arrays-12.statement: You cannot call `push()` on an array that is stored in a `const`.
arrays-12.explain: `const` only means that the variable always holds the same array. You can still add, remove and change its items.
objects.title: Objects
objects.summary: Group related data in objects: read and change properties, write methods, use destructuring and turn objects into JSON.
objects.lesson.0: An **object** groups values that belong together. Each value has a name, called a **key**. Together they form a **property**. You write an object with curly braces and `key: value` pairs, separated by commas.
objects.lesson.2: You read and change a property with a dot, like `user.age`. You add a new property in the same way. A property that does not exist gives `undefined`.
objects.lesson.4: With square brackets, you write the key as a string: `user["name"]`. This is useful when the key is stored in a variable.
objects.lesson.7: A function inside an object is called a **method**. Inside a method, `this` is the object itself, so the method can use the other properties.
objects.lesson.10: **Destructuring** takes properties out of an object and stores them in variables with the same names, all in one line.
objects.lesson.12: `JSON.stringify()` turns an object into a string in the **JSON** format. Programs often use JSON to send data to each other, for example over the internet.
objects.card.2: `this` inside a method is the object
objects-1.explain: `car.brand` reads the property `brand` of the object.
objects-3.explain: The object has no property `age`. A property that does not exist gives `undefined`.
objects-4.explain: `car.key` looks for a property with the name `key`, which does not exist. `car[key]` would use the value of the variable and print `red`.
objects-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `blue`.
objects-5.explain: `settings[name]` uses the value of `name`, which is `"theme"`. `settings.name` looks for a property called `name`.
objects-6.prompt: Build a line that takes `name` and `age` out of `user`.
objects-6.explain: Destructuring of an object uses curly braces: `const { name, age } = user;`.
objects-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Ada is 36`.
objects-7.explain: Add `age` before the destructuring. Otherwise `age` would be `undefined`.
objects-8.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
objects-8.pairs.3: turns the object into a JSON string
objects-9.prompt: The program should print `Hi, I am Max`. Which line has the bug?
objects-9.explain: Inside a method, you reach the other properties through `this`. The fix is `this.name` instead of `name`.
objects-10.explain: JSON puts double quotes around keys and strings and has no spaces.
objects-11.explain: Destructuring stores `4` in `width` and `3` in `height`. `4 * 3` is `12`.
objects-12.statement: Inside a method, `this` is the object that the method belongs to.
objects-12.explain: That is why a method can read and change the other properties with `this.name` or `this.count`.
